items.explanation: The North outmatched the South in people, industry, railroads, and finance — but it did not hold more territory; conquering the vast Confederacy was the Union's central problem.
options: A. The North held more territory than the South
B. The North had more railroad mileage
C. The North had more factories
D. The North had the larger population
items.stem: The North held many advantages at the war's outset EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: Correct — this is the exception. The North did not hold more territory; the Confederacy was vast, and conquering that enormous area was the Union's central military problem.
option_explanations.B: The North did have far more railroad mileage — a real advantage that let it move troops and supplies while Southern railroads crumbled.
option_explanations.C: The North did have far more factories — a real advantage that produced the weapons, uniforms, and supplies a long war required.
option_explanations.D: The North did have the larger population — about 22 million to the South's 9 million — a real advantage in raising armies.

items.explanation: Europe found other cotton, doubted a Confederate victory, and — especially after the Emancipation Proclamation — would not back a slaveholding republic. All three reasons kept Europe out.
options: A. Europe found alternative sources of cotton
B. Europe opposed the Confederacy's defense of slavery
C. Europe doubted the Confederacy could win
D. All of the above
items.stem: European powers withheld diplomatic recognition from the Confederacy because

option_explanations.A: This is true: Europe found alternative cotton sources in Egypt and India, so 'King Cotton' diplomacy failed to force recognition.
option_explanations.B: This is true: European public opinion opposed slavery, and after the Emancipation Proclamation no European power would back a slaveholding republic.
option_explanations.C: This is true: European governments doubted the Confederacy could win its independence, and no one wanted to recognize a losing cause.
option_explanations.D: Correct. All three reasons kept Europe out: alternative cotton supplies, opposition to backing a slaveholding republic, and doubt that the Confederacy could win.

items.explanation: The Enrollment Act let draftees hire substitutes or pay $300 for exemption — a 'rich man's war, poor man's fight' that sparked resentment and the 1863 New York draft riots.
options: A. It opened the army to Black soldiers
B. It swept Irish immigrants into uniform
C. It let the drafted hire substitutes or buy exemption
D. It required martial law to enforce
items.stem: The Union military draft angered many Northerners because

option_explanations.A: The draft's anger was not about Black soldiers entering the army. Black enlistment came through the Emancipation Proclamation and regiments like the 54th Massachusetts — a separate policy from the Enrollment Act's exemptions.
option_explanations.B: Irish immigrants were indeed swept into uniform, but that was not the grievance. The anger was that the wealthy could buy their way out while immigrants and laborers could not.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The Enrollment Act let draftees hire substitutes or pay $300 for exemption — a 'rich man's war, poor man's fight' that sparked bitter resentment and the 1863 New York City draft riots.
option_explanations.D: The draft did not require martial law to enforce. It was enforced by provost marshals through the normal machinery of the Enrollment Act; the grievance was its unfairness, not martial law.

items.explanation: Grant's six-week siege ended July 4, 1863, splitting the Confederacy and giving the Union command of the Mississippi — paired with Gettysburg, the war's turning point.
options: A. It reversed a string of Union defeats that year
B. It opened the road to Atlanta
C. It gave the Union control of the Mississippi River
D. It proved Lee could be beaten in the East
items.stem: Vicksburg was a crucial Union victory because

option_explanations.A: Vicksburg's importance was not reversing a string of defeats. Its significance was strategic: it gave the Union the Mississippi River and split the Confederacy in two.
option_explanations.B: Vicksburg did not open the road to Atlanta. That came a year later, with Sherman's 1864 campaign from Chattanooga.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Grant's six-week siege ended July 4, 1863, giving the Union control of the Mississippi River and splitting the Confederacy — paired with Gettysburg, the war's turning point.
option_explanations.D: Vicksburg did not prove Lee could be beaten in the East. That was Gettysburg's lesson; Vicksburg was a Western theater victory over Pemberton's army.

items.explanation: Copperheads were Northern Democrats who denounced the war as ruinous and demanded peace — Lincoln's most bitter domestic foes.
options: A. Northern Democrats who opposed the war
B. Northern Republicans who wanted Lincoln replaced
C. Northern Democrats who rallied to Lincoln
D. Southern Democrats seeking early negotiations

option_explanations.A: Correct. Copperheads were Northern Democrats who denounced the war as ruinous and demanded a negotiated peace — Lincoln's most bitter domestic opponents.
option_explanations.B: Copperheads were not Republicans at all. The Republicans who pressed Lincoln were the Radicals, who wanted a harsher war policy — the opposite of the Copperheads' peace demands.
option_explanations.C: Copperheads did not rally to Lincoln. Northern Democrats who supported the war were called War Democrats; Copperheads were the peace faction that opposed him.
option_explanations.D: Copperheads were Northerners, not Southerners. They were Northern Democrats — named for the venomous snake — who opposed the war from within the Union.

items.explanation: Scott writes that blockade plus the Mississippi thrust would 'bring them to terms with less bloodshed than by any other plan.' The old general, who had seen war's cost in Mexico, preferred strangulation to a bloody direct invasion -- the passage states his reasoning outright.
options: A. End the rebellion with less bloodshed than a direct invasion
B. Free the enslaved people immediately
C. Provoke European powers to intervene
D. Destroy the cities of the South
items.stem: Scott favored the blockade-and-Mississippi strategy because he believed it would
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"We rely greatly on the sure operation of a complete blockade of the Atlantic and Gulf ports soon to commence. In connection with such a blockade we propose a powerful movement down the Mississippi to the Gulf... the effect would be to isolate the rebellious states and cut off their foreign trade."
—Gen. Winfield Scott, outlining the 'Anaconda Plan,' 1861 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: Correct. Scott writes that blockade plus the Mississippi thrust would 'bring them to terms with less bloodshed than by any other plan' — the old general, who had seen war's cost in Mexico, preferred strangulation to a bloody direct invasion.
option_explanations.B: Scott's plan said nothing about freeing enslaved people immediately. Emancipation as a war aim came later, with the Emancipation Proclamation of 1863.
option_explanations.C: Scott did not want to provoke European intervention. The blockade aimed to cut the South's foreign trade — and with it any reason for Europe to intervene — not to invite it.
option_explanations.D: Scott did not propose destroying Southern cities. His plan was to isolate and squeeze the Confederacy into submission, not to lay waste to its towns.

items.explanation: The North's decisive material edge was industrial: by 1860 it held the great majority of the nation's factory output, railroad mileage, and firearms production -- the arsenal that sustained a long war. Fighting on home ground and a strong cavalry tradition were Southern advantages; Northern opinion was deeply divided (Copperheads).
options: A. Fighting on familiar home territory
B. A unified public opinion behind the war
C. Far greater industrial output and railroad networks
D. A long tradition of cavalry service
items.stem: Which of the following was a major Northern military advantage during the Civil War?
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"We rely greatly on the sure operation of a complete blockade of the Atlantic and Gulf ports soon to commence. In connection with such a blockade we propose a powerful movement down the Mississippi to the Gulf... the effect would be to isolate the rebellious states and cut off their foreign trade."
—Gen. Winfield Scott, outlining the 'Anaconda Plan,' 1861 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: Fighting on familiar home territory was a Southern advantage, not a Northern one — the Confederacy fought a defensive war on ground its soldiers knew.
option_explanations.B: Northern public opinion was not unified behind the war. Copperhead Democrats opposed it, draft riots rocked New York, and Lincoln faced bitter domestic opposition throughout.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The North's decisive material edge was industrial: by 1860 it held the great majority of the nation's factory output, railroad mileage, and firearms production — the arsenal that sustained a long war.
option_explanations.D: A long cavalry tradition was a Southern advantage, not a Northern one — Southern horsemanship gave Confederate cavalry an early edge under leaders like J.E.B. Stuart.

items.explanation: Northern politicians and newspapers jeered at the aging general's slow strangulation scheme -- 'Anaconda Plan' began as mockery from those demanding a quick march on Richmond. Scott was soon eased out, yet the Union eventually executed essentially his design: the blockade plus Grant's drive down the Mississippi.
options: A. it was adopted enthusiastically and at once
B. it was ridiculed as too slow by those demanding quick victory
C. Congress rejected it as unconstitutional
D. critics demanded it be made far harsher
items.stem: Scott's plan was initially received by most Northern political leaders with
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"We rely greatly on the sure operation of a complete blockade of the Atlantic and Gulf ports soon to commence. In connection with such a blockade we propose a powerful movement down the Mississippi to the Gulf... the effect would be to isolate the rebellious states and cut off their foreign trade."
—Gen. Winfield Scott, outlining the 'Anaconda Plan,' 1861 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: The plan was not adopted enthusiastically at once. Politicians and newspapers jeered at the aging general's slow scheme — 'Anaconda Plan' began as mockery.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Northern political leaders ridiculed Scott's strangulation strategy as too slow; they demanded a quick march on Richmond instead. Scott was soon eased out, though the Union eventually executed essentially his design.
option_explanations.C: Congress did not reject the plan as unconstitutional. The objection was strategic — it was too slow — not legal.
option_explanations.D: Critics did not demand the plan be made harsher. They demanded it be faster — a direct strike at Richmond rather than a slow blockade and river campaign.
